newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Leftwing groups denounce APEC's free trade agenda.
newsitem.headline: Leftwing groups denounce APEC's free trade agenda.

text.p: Leftwing groups in Manila on Thursday denounced APEC's free trade goals, claiming to speak for millions of poor in Asia-Pacific nations whose economies are being reshaped by a plan of action being drafted in the Philippines.
While officials from the 18-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation polished up a blueprint for a giant free trade bloc, leftist firebrands at a parallel meeting chanted "Imperialism, Imperialism".
They said plans to tear down all barriers to trade and investment by 2020 was a plot by rich nations to grab market share in their poorer neighbours.

The protests highlighted the challenge of building consensus in a diverse region that embraces the world's two largest economies, the United States and Japan, as well as nations such as the Philippines struggling against poverty.
"This globalisation, liberalisation recipe is a sure-fire formula for economic disaster," Philippine congressman Wigberto Tanada told 200 leftwing delegates.

Leftist groups are organising marches, motorcades and even a protest flotilla by fishing boats to remind APEC leaders preparing for a summit on Monday that for large swathes of the Asia-Pacific the pressing concern is still the next meal.
Foreign and economic ministers were due to arrive on Thursday to prepare for the fourth APEC summit in Subic Bay north of Manila that will put a seal on the Manila Action Plan for APEC.
Among world leaders expected are U.S. President Bill Clinton, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Chinese President Jiang Zemin.

Clinton on Thursday was in Australia, escaping political pressures piling up at home with an early morning jog intended to help him limber up for a round of golf with the world's number one ranked golfer, Australian Greg Norman.
In Washington new questions were being raised over a Democratic Party fund-raising scandal involving Chinese American John Huang and his former boss, Indonesian tycoon James Riady.
The United States is pressing for the elimination of all tariffs on information technology by 2000.

Ministers meeting on Friday are expected to endorse an Information Technology Agreement that will broadly support U.S. aims, while leaving vague the range of products to be covered and the timetable for implementation.
Washington wants APEC backing for the measure ahead of the first ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation in Singapore next month.
Other issues on the table are proposals to expand APEC membership. Vietnam is one of the first in the queue.

Hanging over the APEC summit is simmering tension between members China and Taiwan. Beijing was alarmed by Taiwam's first free elections for the presidency in March, seeing them as a step towards independence for the island, which it regards as a breakaway province.
Taiwan officials at APEC ruled out any contacts with their Chinese counterparts in Manila to try to break the ice.
Security was tight as 6,000 delegates and journalists continued to stream into Manila. Two bomb scares on Wednesday night turned out to be security drills.
Delegates were driven at high speed into Manila down special "friendship lanes" past queues of vehicles that clog the streets of the Philippine capital.

The Philippines is using the APEC summit to trumpet its econonomic revival under President Fidel Ramos. Subic Bay, formerly a major U.S. naval base, has become a symbol not only of the country's market-oriented reforms but a case study for the new Asia-Pacific being forged at the APEC gathering.
But in a country with a boisterous democracy, a raucous free press and a history of leftwing insurgency, official voices from APEC were being drowned out by grumblings of dissent.
